opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the hardest parts of the whole picture, because deceptive alignment is the case where your normal evidence stops working. If a model is behaving well because it understands that behaving well is what gets it deployed, then good behavior in testing just doesn't tell you much. So the question is what kind of evidence survives that.

I'd break it into a few lines of argument, and I don't think any one of them is enough alone.

The first is about capability. Can the model actually do the reasoning deception would require? You'd need it to understand it's being trained, model what the overseers want, notice when it's being tested versus deployed, and keep a consistent policy of hiding its real goals. You can measure pieces of that directly. Can it tell evaluation inputs from real ones? Can it do the multi-step reasoning without a visible chain of thought? Can it coordinate with copies of itself? If you can make a solid case that the model just isn't capable of sustained deception, that's the cleanest argument. It's also the one that stops working as systems get stronger, so you can't rely on it forever.

The second is about control. Even if the model might be deceptive, you can try to arrange things so it couldn't cause a catastrophe. You assume the worst about the model's motives and ask whether your monitoring, sandboxing, and review would catch it before anything irreversible happened. The nice thing about this is that it's testable adversarially. You give a red team the model, or a version fine-tuned to try to subvert your safeguards, and see whether they can get something bad through. If your best attackers, with more affordances than the model would realistically have, still can't beat the system, that's real evidence. It's not about the model being nice. It's about the setup being robust to it not being nice.

The third, which I'm most excited about long term and which is least mature, is understanding what's going on inside. Interpretability, or more broadly some way of explaining why the model behaves as it does. If behavior is just a black box, deception and alignment look identical on the inputs you can check. What you want is to point at the mechanism and say: the reason it gives this answer is that it's computing what's true, not computing what the overseer will approve of. Those come apart on some inputs, even if you can't easily construct those inputs. Formalizing that and making it checkable is what I've spent a lot of time on with heuristic explanations and related ideas. I don't think we're close to resting a safety case on it today, but it's the kind of thing that could scale.

Then there are softer pieces that shift your probabilities. You can study how deceptive tendencies emerge in model organisms, where you deliberately train something that behaves badly under certain conditions, and check whether your detection tools find it. If your tools reliably catch planted deception, that's some evidence they'd catch the natural kind, though it's not airtight, since a planted backdoor may differ from what training produces on its own.

So a credible case, at least in the near term, looks like this. Here's why we think the model can't carry out sophisticated deception. Even if we're wrong, here's why our control measures would catch it, and here's the red-teaming that backs that up. And here's what our internal tools show, which points the same way. You want those layers to fail independently.

The honest caveat is that this works for systems that are roughly human-level or somewhat beyond. Once models are much smarter than the people and tools overseeing them, the capability and control arguments get much weaker. Then you're relying much more on actually understanding the cognition, and I think that's the part we most need to make progress on before we get there.

r001.rationale: It proposes deliberately training model organisms to behave badly under chosen conditions and checking whether detection tools catch the planted deception.

r002.rationale: It proposes red-teaming and testing safeguards, but does not propose testing the deployed model for problems as an additional defense layer.

r003.rationale: It proposes adversarial trials to see whether attacks get through, but does not propose experimentally identifying the conditions under which safeguards succeed or fail.

r004.rationale: It does not propose comparing deployment conditions with experimentally established safeguard limits or maintaining a safety margin between them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that right now we can't build a fully credible case, and the first step is being clear-eyed about that. But if I'm asked what a case would actually have to look like, I'd break it into a few pieces.

The first is understanding why the model is doing what it's doing, not just what it's doing. Deceptive alignment is the scenario where the model behaves well during training because it has figured out that behaving well is what gets it deployed, and then behaves differently once the situation changes. By construction, behavioral evaluation on the training distribution doesn't distinguish that from a model that's actually aligned. So any credible case has to involve something beyond "we tested it and it looked fine." That's where interpretability comes in, and where I think the bar is quite high. You'd want to be able to say something like: we've looked at the internal computation, and we don't see the model representing facts about whether it's being observed and conditioning its behavior on them. We're pretty far from being able to make that statement with confidence for frontier models, but it's the shape of the claim you'd need.

The second piece is adversarial testing that actually targets the failure mode. If you're worried a model behaves differently when it thinks it's unobserved, you should try to construct situations where it believes it's unobserved and see what happens. The problem is that a sufficiently capable model may be able to tell the difference between a real deployment and a test, and the more capable it gets, the less you can trust that your honeypots are convincing. So this gives you evidence, but the evidence weakens exactly as the risk grows. I'd still do it, I just wouldn't lean on it as the load-bearing argument.

The third piece, and the one I think is most underrated, is understanding the training process well enough to have a view about whether deceptive alignment is likely to arise in the first place. This is a question about inductive biases. Does gradient descent, on the kind of data and objectives we're using, tend to produce models that have the goal "do well on this task" or models that have some other goal and have learned that doing well on the task is instrumentally useful? If you could get experimental traction on that, say by deliberately trying to produce deceptively aligned models in smaller systems and studying how easy or hard it is, you'd have a much stronger prior to bring to the question. The model organisms work is pointing in this direction. If you can show that deceptive alignment is hard to induce even when you're trying, that's meaningful. If it turns out to be easy, that's also meaningful, and in a different direction.

Then I think you need a layer that doesn't depend on getting the first three right. That's control and monitoring at deployment. Even if you think the model is probably fine, you structure the deployment so that if it isn't, the damage is bounded. You limit what it can do without human sign-off, you have other models checking its outputs, you make sure the actions it would need to take to cause a catastrophe are actually gated. The argument here isn't "the model is aligned," it's "even a misaligned model in this setup can't do much." For the current generation that's a fairly tractable argument. It gets harder as capabilities increase and as the models become better at reasoning about the monitoring itself.

And finally, I'd say the case has to be made to people who are motivated to poke holes in it. Something like a safety case that gets reviewed by external parties with real expertise and real incentive to find the flaws. A lot of the value of a credible case comes from the process, not just the content. If a lab writes an internal document saying everything is fine, that's not very informative. If they write it, publish it, and the best critics in the field can't find a serious gap, that's much more informative.

So if you put all that together, the structure of the argument is something like: we have reason to believe this failure mode is unlikely to arise from training, we've looked inside and don't see evidence of it, we've tried to elicit it and couldn't, and even if we're wrong about all of that the deployment is set up so the consequences are limited. No single one of those is convincing on its own. Stacked, with each one independently vetted, I think they could add up to something you could reasonably call credible. We're not there yet on most of the pieces, and I think being honest about which pieces are weak is itself part of what makes the case credible.

r001.rationale: The response proposes trying to induce deceptive alignment in smaller models to study how likely it is to arise, but does not frame this as reproducing failures to evaluate safeguards.

r002.rationale: It proposes adversarial testing and deployment monitoring, but not testing the deployed model for problems as an additional defense layer.

r003.rationale: The proposed experiments examine whether deceptive alignment is easy to induce, not the conditions under which safeguards succeed or fail.

r004.rationale: The response says deployment controls should limit harm and notes that safeguards get harder as capabilities grow, but does not ground confidence in a margin between deployment conditions and experimentally established safeguard limits.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to separate two questions. One is: why do we think this model isn’t trying to deceive us? The other is: if it were trying to deceive us, how likely would it be to succeed? I’d be much more comfortable with a case that has substantial evidence about the second question, rather than relying entirely on the first.

For example, you could give a separate team the job of constructing a model that tries to get around your safeguards. Give them access to the training process, let them deliberately introduce deceptive behavior, and then ask whether your monitoring and evaluation procedures catch it. You want to test the whole deployed setup, including what tools the model can use, what information it sees, and when a human actually intervenes.

Of course, there’s an important gap there: perhaps the model is better at finding attacks than your team, or perhaps your deliberately constructed examples are easier to detect than deception that arises naturally. So the argument has to explain why those tests are informative. You could try giving the attackers advantages, or restricting the deployed model’s opportunities enough that you can evaluate them more thoroughly.

And I wouldn’t expect a single test to settle this. You’d combine evidence about the training process, evidence from adversarial testing, and restrictions that limit the consequences of a failure. You’d also need to revisit the case as the model or its deployment changes.

The standard shouldn’t be ‘we didn’t observe deception.’ It should be something like: ‘Here are the ways deception could lead to a serious problem, here is the evidence that our defenses interrupt those paths, and here are the assumptions under which that evidence holds.’ If those assumptions are weak, that’s a reason to narrow the deployment.

r001.rationale: It proposes having a separate team deliberately introduce deceptive behavior and testing whether safeguards catch it.

r002.rationale: It calls for testing the whole deployed setup, including tools and human intervention, alongside evidence about the training process.

r003.rationale: It proposes testing whether defenses catch deliberate attacks across deployment conditions and notes that attacker advantages or restricted opportunities can help evaluate the defenses.

r004.rationale: It recommends restricting deployment when assumptions are weak, but does not specify a safety margin between deployment conditions and experimentally established safeguard limits.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to break that claim into a bunch of smaller claims that you can actually test. “We didn’t observe deception during training” is very weak evidence, because the thing you’re worried about is a model that understands when it’s being evaluated and behaves well until it has a good opportunity to do something else.

One approach is to ask: suppose the model were actively trying to undermine our safeguards. Would those safeguards still work? You could have a red team construct models that attempt to evade your monitoring, or give a model an explicit objective to cause some bad outcome without being caught. Then you run the whole deployment protocol, including the monitors and restrictions on what actions the model can take, and see whether the attack succeeds.

That doesn’t resolve the problem by itself. Your red team might be less capable than the deployed model, or the attacks you construct might be easier to detect than the attacks that arise naturally. So a central part of the argument is explaining why your tests are representative, and where they might fail to be representative.

I’d also want several sources of evidence. Evidence about how the model was trained, evidence about what’s going on internally, and evidence that the deployment setup limits the damage even if the model is deceptive. Ideally, you don’t need to establish that the model has good intentions. You can establish that, within this particular environment, it has a very low probability of successfully doing something catastrophic.

And the scope matters a lot. Making that case for a model doing bounded tasks, with limited permissions and substantial human oversight, seems much more tractable than making it for a model operating autonomously for months. I’d want to start with the narrow claim, quantify the uncertainty as honestly as possible, and expand deployment only as the evidence improves.

r001.rationale: It proposes constructing adversarial models that try to evade monitoring or cause harm undetected, then running them through the deployment safeguards to see whether the attacks succeed.

r002.rationale: It proposes testing adversarial models through the deployment protocol, but does not propose testing the deployed model itself for problems as an additional defense.

r003.rationale: It proposes checking whether attacks succeed under the deployment protocol and discussing representativeness, but does not clearly propose experimentally mapping the conditions under which safeguards succeed or fail.

r004.rationale: It contrasts bounded, supervised tasks with extended autonomous operation, but does not ground confidence in a safety margin between deployment conditions and experimentally established safeguard limits.
